hard.q: Scegli la domanda corretta: «Quando la chiami?»
hard.e: Parola interrogativa + verbo + soggetto; davanti a je la -t cade; come complemento oggetto serve haar, non zij.

g.Wanneer belt je haar?: davanti a je la t cade
g.Wanneer je belt haar?: il verbo deve venire prima del soggetto
g.Wanneer bel je zij?: zij è soggetto: come oggetto serve haar

hard.q: Hoeveel kinderen ___ Tom en Sofie? — Drie: twee meisjes en een jongen.
hard.e: Il soggetto Tom en Sofie è plurale: hebben. Il verbo viene subito dopo hoeveel kinderen.

hard.q: Perché prendete il treno per Bruxelles?
a: Waarom nemen jullie de trein naar Brussel
Waarom pakken jullie de trein naar Brussel
Waarom neemt u de trein naar Brussel
Waarom pakt u de trein naar Brussel
Waarom neemt ge de trein naar Brussel
Waarom pakt ge de trein naar Brussel

hard.q: Quanto costano tre chili di formaggio?
hard.e: Di solito il verbo va al plurale (kosten; con le misure è accettato anche kost), ma kilo resta al singolare dopo un numero, e non serve "di": drie kilo kaas.
Waar all'inizio, vandaan alla fine; il verbo al plurale komen va prima del soggetto.
Verbo prima di je (senza -t), poi il pronome oggetto haar e niet alla fine.

en.note:
Yes/no questions: the verb goes first

English builds most questions with "do" (Do you speak Dutch?). Dutch has no helper like that: you simply swap the order and put the verb in first position, before the subject.

statementquestion
Hij spreekt Frans.Spreekt hij Frans?
Jij woont in Gent.Woon je in Gent?
U komt morgen.Komt u morgen?

Remember the rule from unit 2: in front of je/jij the -t of the verb drops.

Questions with a question word

The order is: question word + verb + subject + the rest.

DutchEnglishexample
wiewhoWie is dat?
watwhatWat doe je?
waarwhereWaar woon je?
wanneerwhenWanneer kom je?
waaromwhyWaarom leer je Nederlands?
hoehowHoe heet je?
hoeveelhow much, how manyHoeveel kost dat?

Welke or welk?

"Which" is welke, except in front of a singular het-word, where it's welk: welk huis? but welke fiets? and welke huizen?

Where from: waar … vandaan

"Where are you from?" is Waar kom je vandaan? Waar goes at the start and vandaan at the end of the sentence, a bit like English "Where do you come from?"

Hoe heet je?

To ask someone's name you use hoe (how), not wat: Hoe heet je? Literally "how are you called?", not "what is your name?".

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Looking for a "do" helper: Doe je wonen in Gent? → Woon je in Gent?
  • Keeping statement order after the question word: Waar je woont? → Waar woon je?
  • Translating "what's your name" word for word: Wat heet je? → Hoe heet je?
en.vlaams: You'll often hear "Hoe gaat het met u?" (How are you?) even in informal settings. A typical answer is "Goed, merci!": Flemish people often say merci for thank you, alongside "dank u".

items.e: You say Hoe heet je? (literally: how are you called).
Verb first, and the -t drops in front of je. No "do" or "are" helper: just Werk je.
Waarom leer je Nederlands? Dutch uses the simple present here.

drills.e: Verb first, and no t in front of je.

g.Je woont in Gent?: intonation only: you need to invert
g.Woont je in Gent?: the t drops in front of je
g.In Gent je woont?: the verb must come before the subject

0.t: Where do you live? In Ghent.

5.t: How much is it? Five euros.

hard.q: ___ kinderen wonen in Gent? — De kinderen van Tom en Sofie.
hard.e: het kind is a het-word, but in the plural it's always welke: welke kinderen.

g.Wie: who (on its own, without a noun)

hard.tt: Which children live in Ghent? — Tom and Sofie's children.

hard.q: Pick the correct question: "When are you calling her?"
hard.e: Question word + verb + subject; the -t drops in front of je; as the object you need haar, not zij (her, not she).

g.Wanneer belt je haar?: the t drops in front of je
g.Wanneer je belt haar?: the verb must come before the subject
g.Wanneer bel je zij?: zij is a subject (she): as the object you need haar

hard.q: Hoeveel kinderen ___ Tom en Sofie? — Drie: twee meisjes en een jongen.
hard.e: The subject Tom en Sofie is plural: hebben. The verb comes right after hoeveel kinderen, with no "do" helper.
hard.tt: How many children do Tom and Sofie have? — Three: two girls and a boy.

hard.q: Why are you guys taking the train to Brussels?
a: Waarom nemen jullie de trein naar Brussel
Waarom pakken jullie de trein naar Brussel
Waarom neemt u de trein naar Brussel
Waarom pakt u de trein naar Brussel
Waarom neemt ge de trein naar Brussel
Waarom pakt ge de trein naar Brussel
hard.e: Waarom + verb + subject: nemen jullie. Going to a city: naar Brussel.

hard.q: How much do three kilos of cheese cost?
hard.e: The verb is usually plural (kosten; with measures kost is also accepted), but kilo stays singular after a number, and there's no "of": drie kilo kaas.
Waar at the start, vandaan at the end; the plural verb komen comes before the subject.
No "do" in Dutch: the verb comes before je (without -t), then the object pronoun haar, and niet at the end.
